idiom_name: hand-written AppContext passed by reference; thread_local for process-wide services
implementation_notes: Without a component tree there is nothing to hang an ambient value on, so the default C++ realization is a small context struct (services, configuration, request identity) passed by reference into the functions that need it, and a thread_local instance for values that really are ambient per thread. The classic provider/consumer structure is still justified when a callback chain would otherwise have to grow a parameter at every level - for example logging or trace context inside a library callback - and even then the value should be immutable and set once per thread.
pitfalls: thread_local values are per thread and there is no scope exit: a worker in a pool keeps the last request's value until it is overwritten, and nothing warns you.
A context object that stores references must not outlive its referents - passing AppContext by value into an object that lives longer than the caller creates dangling references.
A global context object constructed in another translation unit risks the static initialisation order fiasco; use function-local statics or inject it from main.

variants.name: Explicit context object plus thread_local for genuinely ambient values

variants.name: std::pmr memory_resource propagation (value propagated by construction)
variants.implementation_notes: The standard library's own downward-propagation idiom: a memory_resource is attached to a polymorphic_allocator, and allocator-aware containers pass it on to their elements through uses-allocator construction (scoped_allocator_adaptor generalises the same mechanism), so nested containers allocate from the same resource without any constructor naming it explicitly. Choose this when the ambient value is a resource or policy that must reach every allocation in a subtree; for arbitrary application data, use the explicit context object variant instead.
pitfalls: The resource must outlive every container created with it - a monotonic_buffer_resource destroyed first leaves those containers with a dangling resource pointer.
monotonic_buffer_resource does not return individual deallocations upstream, so it fits short-lived request arenas, not long-lived containers.
Allocator equality is delegated to memory_resource::is_equal (operator== was removed in C++20), so containers bound to different resources are not interchangeable.
